speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Like its predecessor, the new portal included a People Search function.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This function allowed users to search for and select the individuals associated with registered business entities whose information they wished to access through the purchase of a People Profile.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there is a People Search function and the People Profile function.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The People Search function is generally available to everyone, anyone.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Minister for Digital Development and Information, Mrs Josephine Teo, and the Second Minister for Finance, Ms Indranee Rajah, held a media conference on 19 December 2024, during which they apologised for the anxiety caused.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They explained what had happened and the Government's intent to change the existing practice of using partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ministers Josephine Teo and Indranee Rajah also made Ministerial Statements to this House on 8 January 2025 and responded to requests for clarifications from Members.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To thoroughly review the matter, the Prime Minister directed the Head of the Civil Service to set up a Panel to review the Government's policy on the responsible use of NRIC numbers where it pertained to the Bizfile portal; second, to determine what led to the Bizfile incident; and to identify learning points so that similar incidents do not recur.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Panel also reviewed the design and implementation of the People Search function and the response to the incident by ACRA and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI), from the time public concerns arose on 12 December 2024 until the People Search function was disabled on 13 December 2024.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: After studying the report carefully, the Prime Minister agreed with its findings, its assessment of the shortcomings and the learning points identified.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He said that the Government would take the lessons to heart to improve its processes and strive to do better.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He directed that the report be released to the public and for the matter to be deliberated in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: ACRA and MDDI have also accepted the findings and released separate media statements on their follow-up actions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is set out on the first page of the handout, which is the Annex to the Panel's report.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Josephine Teo had addressed these issues in her Ministerial Statement on 8 January 2025 to this House.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, allow me to recap these issues briefly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The NRIC number allows the individual to be referred to uniquely and definitively.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is important to definitively refer to an individual by using the full NRIC number when required by law and for other purposes, such as for medical procedures and business transactions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, the NRIC number had also become used by some organisations, not just to definitively refer to the individual, but also based just on the NRIC number, to carry out important and sensitive actions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The use of the NRIC number in this way is unsafe, because the person's NRIC number is likely to be already known to other persons or organisations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Some organisations and people had also come to assume that the use of partial NRIC numbers means that the full NRIC number is thereby concealed and protected.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The use of partial NRIC numbers, therefore, neither meets the need to have a definitive way of referring uniquely to an individual, nor does it offer effective protection from the full NRIC number becoming known.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To address these issues, the former Smart Nation and Digital Government Office (SNDGO), now part of MDDI, commenced a policy review in 2022.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The review determined that we should take steps to stop the incorrect use of NRIC numbers for authentication and also move organisations away from the use of partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This would allow NRIC numbers to be returned to their proper use as unique identifiers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministers overseeing SNDGO were responsible for deciding the policy direction on the use of NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Ministers endorsed the policy intent of returning NRIC numbers to their proper use as unique identifiers and the broad implementation approach to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Permanent Secretaries of SNDGO, and subsequently MDDI, had overall responsibility for the implementation plans in accordance with the guidance from the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: SNDGO, and subsequently MDDI, knew the transition would take time and planned for the public sector to take the lead on both: (a) stopping the use of NRIC numbers for authentication; and (b) moving away from the use of partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It also started developing plans for public education and private sector engagements on the proper use of NRIC numbers and the risks of using partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, with that background, I refer Members to the second page of the handout, which is on the timeline of key events.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The full listing is in the table in the report.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: SNDGO had planned for the public sector to move first in a phased approach.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: MDDI conducted a briefing on 16 July 2024 for agencies, including ACRA, on the CM, and answered their questions on it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The video recording of the briefing and MDDI's responses to agencies' Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) were disseminated to agencies the next day.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: ACRA subsequently sought clarifications via email from MDDI on how the CM applied to the display of NRIC numbers in the search results of People Search in the new Bizfile portal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, communications between the two sides were not clear.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, MDDI had intended that agencies could continue to use partial NRIC numbers for their existing external-facing use cases, but were not to introduce new use cases of partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To MDDI, ACRA's Bizfile People Search function was considered an existing use case because it was a service that was already existing in the old portal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: MDDI had also assumed that when agencies stopped using partial NRIC numbers, they would consider if NRIC numbers even remained necessary for those use cases.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This would be in line with existing requirements under the Government's Instruction Manual on Information Communications Technology and Smart Systems Management (IM8).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Panel found that a confluence of several shortcomings on the part of both MDDI and ACRA, and how they had interacted with each other on this issue, led to the incident.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, the Panel found that MDDI should have been clearer in its policy communications in its July 2024 CM.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: MDDI and ACRA staff did not realise that ACRA had misunderstood how the July 2024 CM applied to the new Bizfile portal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Specifically, MDDI should have explained key terms and phrases in the CM more clearly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Although MDDI did make efforts to brief agencies on the requirements of the July 2024 CM and disseminated the video recording of the briefing as well as the FAQs to them, the relevant documents were not appended to the CM.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, if one referred to the CM, one would not have seen the other clarifications arising from the session that MDDI had with the agencies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, there were internal shortcomings within ACRA in sharing and acting on the information from MDDI on the July 2024 CM.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The FAQs mentioned earlier were not properly disseminated within ACRA by the officers who had attended the briefing and the officers who had received the video and the email of what had happened.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this contributed to ACRA's continued misinterpretation of the July 2024 CM and resulted in them making decisions based on incomplete information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These FAQs would, for example, have alerted ACRA that stopping the use of partial NRIC numbers did not mean showing full NRIC numbers in every case, and agencies could decide to drop the use of NRIC numbers altogether.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, the Panel found that MDDI should have paid more attention to the implementation plan for new use cases of partial NRIC numbers that were more complex, such as public registries.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Panel found that, in directing agencies to stop new use cases of partial NRIC numbers, MDDI did not differentiate between simpler use cases, like one-to-one correspondence between public agencies and members of the public, and more complex use cases, like public registries, which could potentially disclose a large amount of data to third parties performing searches.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: ACRA, as the national business registry of Singapore, is one such public registry.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One of ACRA's functions is to provide public access to certain information in the registry, so as to maintain corporate transparency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The standard approach for public registries is to have safeguards, such as a paywall, so that, as far as possible, access to the needed information from the registry is available only to users for whom the service is intended.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But there is also often a search function for the registry, before these safeguards, which is open to everyone to narrow down the information in the registry which the user wishes to access, and agencies have to determine how much to reveal when someone performs a search without having to go through safeguards, such as a paywall, for the information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For such complex use cases, additional guidance from MDDI would have helped agencies decide whether disclosing full NRIC numbers was necessary, and if so, determine what safeguards should be put in place.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In February 2024, five months earlier, ACRA had planned a change to its People Profile – the part after the paywall – to only provide partial NRIC numbers instead of the full NRIC numbers, which it had all along been providing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At that time, SNDGO had advised ACRA on the wider move towards stopping public agencies from using partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Bizfile users had also given feedback to ACRA that full NRIC numbers were needed for corporate transparency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, in view of this feedback and ACRA's exchange with SNDGO, ACRA decided to continue providing the full NRIC numbers in the People Profile function instead of making its proposed changes to partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this is the People Profile function, which is after the paywall, and these were events and discussions in February, five months before the events that occurred.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this exchange with SNDGO in February gave ACRA the impression that the policy intent was to "unmask" all partial NRIC numbers, which was not the case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But that was ACRA's frame of mind when interpreting how the July 2024 CM should be applied to the People Search function in the new Bizfile portal, specifically whether to continue providing partial NRIC numbers or to change to providing full NRIC numbers instead to the part before the paywall.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Nonetheless, even if ACRA was under the mistaken impression that the July 2024 CM required them to disclose full NRIC numbers in People Search, ACRA ought to still have, as required by IM8, assessed the proper balance between the public interest in sharing full NRIC numbers, which was to promote corporate transparency, and the competing public interest in ensuring that full NRIC numbers were not too readily accessible.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Fifth, the review found that certain security features for the People Search function were not adequately implemented for the new Bizfile portal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: After disabling the People Search function, ACRA requested that the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) review the security features of the People Search function.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this was after the fact, after the People Search function had already been launched.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: ACRA is following up with the vendor and considering all its available options.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Without prejudice to any such options, the Panel noted that ACRA remains ultimately accountable for the implementation of the People Search function, even though it had contracted this to its vendor.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The sixth and last finding of the Panel was that the incident management after public concerns on the Bizfile portal surfaced on 12 December 2024 should have been better.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Doing so would have addressed public concerns in a more timely manner.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The public communications and response to public concerns should also have been better coordinated and clearer.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And in hindsight, the Government should have made clear to the public at the outset that moving away from the use of partial NRIC numbers did not automatically mean using full NRIC numbers in every case or disclosing them on a large scale.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Panel noted that the incident took place before MDDI had begun public education and engagement on the proper use of NRIC numbers as a unique identifier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If you recall, the implementation of this was in the public sector and the engagement of the private sector had not begun yet.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this exacerbated public concerns when full NRIC numbers were easily searchable and accessible in the People Search function, since many members of the public would not have been familiar with the issues associated with the use of NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Panel was of the view that it would have been better for MDDI to have embarked on public education and engagement earlier than what it had planned.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Having reviewed it, I agree with the findings.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I had stated earlier, ACRA and MDDI have both accepted the Panel's findings and are following up to address the issues identified, as set out in their respective media statements.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Beyond the agencies involved, this incident offers valuable and important lessons for the wider Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: To meet changing circumstances and new challenges, the Public Service will need to continually update its policies and practices.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Some of these changes will not be straightforward.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: How we communicate and implement them will be critical.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Bizfile incident demonstrates that close coordination and careful attention to detail are required.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Sometimes, it is a single issue, but at other times, it can be a confluence of factors that can lead to such incidents.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The lessons that the Panel has identified will be disseminated across the whole of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Agencies are expected to take them on board and apply them to their work to avoid similar incidents from recurring.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The political office holders overseeing ACRA as well as the Smart Nation work in MDDI have overall responsibility for the organisations under their charge.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this is regardless of whether they had specific or direct responsibility for the actions that led to the shortcomings that occurred.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this distinction between an overall responsibility that political office holders have for the organisations under their charge and the specific or direct responsibility for the actions that led to the shortcomings that occurred.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the Public Service level, the Permanent Secretaries of SNDGO, and subsequently MDDI, were responsible for implementing the policy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Chief Executive of ACRA was responsible for the new Bizfile portal's design and implementation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: While the Panel did not find any evidence of deliberate wrongdoing or wilful inaction by the ACRA and MDDI officers involved in this incident, the shortcomings identified, including ACRA's contravention of IM8, should have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: While the Panel's report serves as a reference, any disciplinary action, if warranted in relation to individual officers, will need to be conducted in accordance with the applicable frameworks and processes in the respective public agencies involved, and this is only proper.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Public Service Division, MDDI and ACRA have taken into account the findings of the Panel and have thus reviewed the roles, responsibilities and actions of the relevant officers involved in the shortcomings highlighted in the report.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These officers include those whose actions contributed directly to the shortcomings, as well as senior management who were responsible for providing oversight and guidance to the officers and are responsible for the proper functioning of their organisations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The cost of any financial penalties would ultimately have to be borne by the public purse if we impose a financial penalty on a public agency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And therefore, such penalties would not be meaningful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Instead, as I have stated, the necessary actions will be taken against the officers responsible.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The PSGA is designed with that in mind.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Given the range and complexity of public services, from time to time, mistakes will be made.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If there is misconduct or malicious intent, we will deal with it severely and those involved will be punished.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Where there had been no malicious or wilful wrongdoing, due consideration should be given to whether the officers had acted in good faith when we decide on what actions to take.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And most importantly, the lessons arising from the incident must be learnt and internalised, not only by the officers involved or their agencies, but by the Public Service as a whole, so that they are not repeated.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Maintaining that trust is, therefore, central to how we operate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When things go wrong, we are upfront with Singaporeans on where we have fallen short.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We conduct thorough reviews and make improvements to our systems and processes to serve Singaporeans better while remaining fair to our officers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now have clarifications on the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I can see that there are many Members wanting to seek clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I would like to take this opportunity to remind Members that pursuant to Standing Order 23, Members may seek clarifications on the Ministerial Statement, but no debate should be allowed.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Members can seek clarifications by way of asking questions.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If any preamble is required and if it takes too long, I will interject and ask you to get straight to asking your clarifications.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I seek Members' understanding to keep your clarifications clear and concise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will ask the same of the Senior Minister in his responses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The questions are follow-ups from my Parliamentary Question filed for the 7 January 2025 Sitting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When did they send it and what was MDDI's response?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question is on ACRA's conversation with MDDI.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It started in February 2024 and it concerned the People Profile function, not the People Search function.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It begs the question: what clarification was sought by ACRA and what was MDDI's response?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it would appear that the new Bizfile portal already was going to continue what the old Bizfile portal was providing to the public: masked NRIC numbers in the People Search function.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it would be helpful to understand what clarifications were sought, because at this point it seems like MDDI confirming to ACRA that it can continue to display masked NRIC numbers in the People Search function "for now", but that it should be prepared for eventual unmasking at a point when MDDI was going to issue future guidance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, at that point, 30 July, it would seem everybody is ad idem on the way forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, this I think is the point which begs further questions – what went wrong after this point?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once again, there is emphasis in the report on paragraph 7 of the CM and the confusion, and Senior Minister has explained how new business processes were misunderstood by ACRA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But paragraph 9, as I alluded to, makes it quite clear that ACRA, in this case, was supposed to provide MDDI a list of their existing correspondence with members of the public using masked NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, that really is the subject of my question: when was that done?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The final question is, at what point did the senior leadership of ACRA fully reviewed the new Bizfile portal before it went public?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, did they assess this balance at any point in time?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is very useful and he should also understand the conclusions that were arrived at in the report and what I had just said.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, he has identified all the misunderstandings in the communication between the two agencies which led to this unfortunate incident.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, this is described in the report as well as in my speech just now.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The two were communicating with each other but they had different frames of mind and therefore, they went away with different understandings of what the CM said and also different understandings of the communications and emails that they had with each other.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In spite of the fact that they had communicated with each other, each went away thinking that they had put their point across clearly and each went away thinking that the other understood what was to be done and what was meant.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Did ACRA send all the instances and so forth?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am sure they have, but the relevant point is that they were communicating on this particular instance and had a gap in understanding between the two.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They probably did, but as I pointed out, and as the Panel pointed out, they did not make a proper assessment of the balance between their function of making such a registry available and conveniently so to users, and the need to manage the access to information in such a search function.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that was a shortcoming on the part of ACRA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Government agencies store, access and handle personal information of Singaporeans in engagements and provision of various Government services and with digitisation, what assurances can be given to Singaporeans on the proper handling of personal data by Government agencies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because it is not just about policies, it is not just about rules; it is about that balance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I actually worry that it may come to the point of everyone being so afraid to move forward because of that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given this incident and the learning from this instance, it may lead to everyone being overly cautious.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I need to understand what will be done across the Government to help our officers move forward and be able to make that right judgement call.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not an easy problem to address.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, some of the things that are in PDPA today, were originally already in the public sector's rules for data governance in IM8, even before PDPA was announced.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And some of the things that were eventually enacted in PDPA and the guidance provided by the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) were also adopted in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But there are a couple of important differences between the two and I will take this opportunity to explain what they are.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First of all, there is no expectation within the private sector that different private sector corporations interact with one another and share data with one another, purportedly to serve the customer better.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, private sector agencies are quite protective of the data that they have because they see that as a competitive advantage, and we also do not allow private sector organisations to sell their data to others for profit.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, by and large, they do not share with others.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We sometimes hear, in Parliament also, "You already know this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Why do you keep on asking me for it?" So, in order to serve residents better, we do share data and this is allowed in the PSGA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, you apply for a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat, access your Central Provident Fund (CPF) account and all those kind of things, it is shared and available.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If someone applies for social service support, that information is available so that the person in a distressed situation already does not have to keep on providing the same information again.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the financial penalties arise from actions taken against individual officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the PDPA, originally, there were no specified penalties against individuals.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there is always a mirroring between the two and there are differences between the two.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First of all, the public sector does have a very strong and robust system for the management of data and the sharing of data, and for taking action against persons who contravene them.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Should this cause persons to become overly careful?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think that it is always a possibility whenever an incident such as this arises.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But that is why it is important to identify the shortcomings clearly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Do not go in with a big bazooka and flatten everybody, but differentiate between the responsibilities of the individuals.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Individuals who are responsible, they have to be held to account, but we must do so in a well-balanced and fair way to the individuals.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is the approach that we take and which we will continue to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the answer is already given by the Minister, please do not repeat the clarification.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I read in that paragraph, where in the reply from MDDI to ACRA, it states that "ACRA can continue to display masked NRIC numbers in the People Search function for now".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And it continues to say that it should be prepared for the "eventual unmasking of the NRIC number".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister whether that remains the policy position – the eventual unmasking of the NRIC number?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And in the case of the People Search function, what is the direction ahead?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Would ACRA eventually stop displaying the masked NRIC number?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Would the full NRIC number be shown in some way, with some controls or with some safeguards?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second clarification is related to page 16 for the chronology of key events.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The report mentioned that ACRA did have internal deliberations about the risk of showing full NRIC numbers in the People Search function.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It shows that ACRA did have concerns, at least, at the working level, but they went ahead because they misunderstood the instructions from the July 2024 CM.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask if there is a deeper issue here, where an agency felt compelled to just go ahead with the launch even though internally, they have some serious concerns or reservations on the public implications?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And whether does the Public Service have the mechanism where officers at the working level who may have spotted a potential high-risk situation, for example, in the upcoming implementation, are able to flag out these concerns and get attention from the management?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If I may just say what has happened to the People Search function, the part before the paywall.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Liang has also read the report very, very carefully – and I am glad that he has done so – and identified certain places where there were gaps.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, they communicated with each other and in the communication that Mr Liang cited, that showed how the two of them misunderstood each other – what is new, what is existing, there was a gap in understanding.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Also, what does stopping the use of partial NRIC numbers mean?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Does it mean that where you had partial NRIC numbers before, you just go and use full NRIC numbers?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there was a gap there in communication between the two agencies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The question that Mr Liang asked is, is there a process for making sure that agencies can communicate and do this?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And if there is a problem and there is an issue, they should engage with each other and thrash that out thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I think that is one of the important lessons that we have learnt from this case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two clarifications for the Senior Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, I found what he said about the overall accountability of Ministers very interesting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He mentioned that the two Ministers involved would have this incident taken into account by the Prime Minister in his assessment of their overall performance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the fact is the Prime Minister is the Minister for Finance and ACRA is a Statutory Board within the Ministry of Finance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, how does that work as far as the Prime Minister is concerned?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Because he is also overall responsible for ACRA, in that sense.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second clarification is about the report's shortcoming number six, which talks about shortcomings in incident management after the public concerns were raised on 12 December.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am personally aware that it is a reality in the Civil Service, and probably private sector, that in December, there are many staff that are on annual leave, we expect them to clear their leave.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And December is usually a time when there are less staff around.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to ask him whether this aspect of key decision-makers not being so readily available, did it feature at all in causing any delays in the incident response?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And does he think that this could be a potential issue, even if it is not an issue in this case?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But to the Panel which reviewed the thing, it was not an acceptable excuse or reason.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that was not something which the Panel took into account – and I think rightly so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But he has to delegate his responsibilities to Ministers who are responsible for Ministries, agencies and functions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is part of the Prime Minister's role.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the Prime Minister tried to be responsible for everything, he would not be able to function at all.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One of the responsibilities of the Prime Minister is to know when he should delegate and when he should intervene.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I hope that Ms Sylvia Lim appreciates that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am also glad to note that Ms Sylvia Lim takes accountability, especially accountability of leaders of organisations, as something which is very serious, and which should be accepted when mistakes are made.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think there have been useful lessons drawn.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because in this case, I think there was a time gap at the beginning, so it allowed a lot of doubts and questions from the public to foment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With digitalisation, information and speculations got worse as a result of that; it did not quite help with that sense of public anxiety.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I wanted to ask if there would be someone or some body to coordinate this going forward, arising from this incident.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second is that I think quite clearly from the report as well as the questions to and fro so far, there has been no malicious intent, no deliberate wilful inaction or action.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was really everyone trying their best to do what they think is right.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Government business gets more complex, there are so many issues at hand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the one hand, ensuring that discipline is taken for errors being done and continuing to strengthen public trust, but on the other hand, continuing to encourage public officers to take calculated risks when necessary so that innovations can still happen, so that things can still move forward, and not to always be worried about what ifs and do not do anything at all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I do not think that will serve us well as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because from the report, I feel a bit worried – are we going to hammer them too much?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because that may not be sending the right signal to the broader Public Service as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Lastly, which pertains to a question that I had asked as a supplementary question during the previous Sitting.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If this is not the right platform for me to ask this, I will file a question separately.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: She has also read the report very thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is an existing process within the Government for actually coordinating across.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is the Committee of Permanent Secretaries, which meets regularly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They discuss issues of importance and issues where coordination between Ministries and agencies should take place.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But apart from that, although the digital world, as Ms Tin correctly points out, spins faster, we also use digital means very often in communicating with each other.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am sure that among the Permanent Secretaries, they will communicate with each other.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They probably have their own address group, where things which are important, which have to be acted on quickly, are communicated with each other.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, because in this day and age, people also travel a lot, so wherever they are in the world, they will also know what is happening.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is a faster process as well in disseminating information and also making sure that things are understood.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should say that by and large, the Public Service actually works very well and coordinates very well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Instances like this do take place, but they are, fortunately, few and far between.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, how do we deal with instances like this and the officers who have come short in their performance?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Ms Tin, and Ms Jessica Tan also, pointed out quite importantly, we should not come down like a tonne of bricks on officers for issues like this, even if they have become public and have caused public anxiety.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We should deal with them fairly and in accordance with the Public Sector's disciplinary processes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is something which I think will give assurance to our officers that just because the thing has become publicly known and caused some anxiety, that we will come down on them in an unfair way.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have to evaluate what they did, what they did not do, what they should have done, what was the intent behind it and then decide on the appropriate action to be taken.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is the way that we should continue to deal with the Public Service so that our Public Service will continue to do all the things that they need to do for us, including taking calculated risks, if they need to, but not take risks dangerously.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, these are things which we should continue to be able to do with our public officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I should explain what is the difference between authentication and using an identifier because there is still a little bit of confusion.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: All of us have an email address and quite often we even use our own name as the email address.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We want the people whom we interact with to know our email address so that they can contact us.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the email address is an identifier of one form and in fact, it is unique because the email service provider has to have the unique names, otherwise it will go to the wrong person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, you actually make your email address available to others.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But for authentication purposes, it is quite different.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: You do not tell your password to others.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is something which you keep for yourself and your email service provider knows.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there is a difference between an identifier and an authentication.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is an example in which most people will understand that, yes, you can use your name as your email address.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is not insecure, and it is very often convenient and expected.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But please do not use your name as your password or your NRIC as your password because, a good number of people know it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is the difference between the two.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have asked two Parliamentary Questions on the same topic in January.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Once it is being harvested, that bell cannot be unrung.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, and I have read the report, it mentions that ACRA outsourced the portal security to the portal vendor.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The vendor then outsourced security penetration tests to a security reviewer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And yet, when GovTech came in, they discovered that the security features were not adequately implemented.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But in any situation, each organisation and each leader has to make the decision based on the information that he has and is able to obtain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, that is one of the requirements of IM8 and which organisations often find a little bit too prescriptive and overbearing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But that is a necessity and for the reasons that Dr Tan has pointed out.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I should say that the Government does not try to build every IT system itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are very reputable IT companies and vendors out there which the Government should make use of.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And there are also very reputable IT security companies out there, some of them are at the leading edge of IT security, which the Government should also make use of.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we should not and do not need to try to do everything ourselves.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And in the evaluation of whom to assign or whom to award the tenders to, these are taken into account.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But, of course, just as the Government can make mistakes sometimes, the IT vendors too, are not perfect, as we know.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Even IT security companies or companies which sell IT security as their main product have made mistakes and been penetrated in an embarrassing way before.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That means, if you do find a bug or you do find a way in which you can penetrate a Government system, you let us know, and there is a bounty for it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But we also do, from time to time, have a hunting season.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, for certain of our systems, we invite white hatters to attack those systems.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And then, we also have a bounty system for that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I am very careful with what I am saying, because as I pointed out, ACRA is keeping all its options open with regard to the IT vendor.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But ultimately, the organisation which owns the system, which is ACRA, has ultimate responsibility for it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I have three clarifications for the Senior Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the report was not submitted to ACRA directly from the reviewer, but it was, in fact, the vendor who submitted the report on the test on its own product.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears to me as if this process has huge potential for abuse.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does it meet with the governance standards for the public sector?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second clarification is: it is obvious from the report that ACRA did realise that there is a conflict between its understanding of the July CM with its obligations under IM8 and PSGA.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why did ACRA prioritise compliance with the July CM over compliance with IM8 and PSGA?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And will there be instruction or guidelines given to organisations how they are to deal with such situations when they find them themselves in apparent positions of conflict?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, it would appear from the report that ACRA sought clarification primarily over emails.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it not be better to have a conversation or a meeting over this to sort out any misunderstandings?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My final clarification is: in paragraph 26 of the report, the Committee noted that we cannot just look at the incident itself but also go upstream.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But think the Committee did not go upstream enough.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to go back and look at the decision to restrict the collection and the use of full NRIC number, which actually led to the creation of masked NRIC numbers, which then created a false sense of security and led to NRICs being used as authenticators even in the public sector.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, have we reviewed that policy decision to find out what are the learning points and if so, what are they?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I would commend Annex A of the report to Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I said, there is an issue with that because it is not sufficient to identify a person or to definitively refer to a person when that need is there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And the belief that using partial NRIC numbers, you can be more relaxed with it, because it is a partial NRIC number, it is not a full NRIC number.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But you cannot be more relaxed with that because, in fact, the full NRIC number is easily discoverable.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, these are problems and issues which arose over time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not think it is because of the rules with regard to collection, use and disclosure of full NRIC numbers that led to this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Those rules on the collection, use and disclosure of full NRIC numbers I think still make sense.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That particular guidance also pointed to people using NRIC numbers for things like lucky draws and so on – it was quite unnecessary – and also whether or not you should collect and retain a person's NRIC card, not just his NRIC number.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And it could have led to the practice of people using partial NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is also a practice which has serious downsides.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, yes, I would commend Annex A to Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is something which ACRA should have considered to strike the right balance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They did to some extent but, I think, the full appreciation was not there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Yes, it is, but, you know, nowadays with digital ability to communicate with each other in email, you can do so quite quickly as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Setting up a meeting can take more time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I do not think that was the fundamental issue.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think I have answered all of Ms Poa's questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Speaker, I thank the Senior Minister for his explanation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 4 of the report highlighted that MDDI's July 2024 CM lacked clarity, leading to misunderstanding in implementation by ACRA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, could Senior Minister elaborate on the steps taken to enhance clarity in future communications to prevent similar incidents?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And secondly, how do we strengthen the clearance and approval processes within the Ministry to prevent similar issues from happening in the future, especially of such a misunderstanding, especially when it pertains to issues across different agencies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I think this is quite important because, as we move forward, the issues that the Government is dealing with is going to be more complex and it involves much more agencies coming together to solve similar issues.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, the issues that Government has to deal with have become more complex and particularly, in the digital age where things are moving so fast.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, things which were adequate two years ago for the digital age may not be adequate today, or you anticipate that they would not be adequate in a year or two.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Some of the security features that we had were adequate in the past but may not be adequate today and in the future, and we have to keep on evolving and changing; and therefore, when we make such changes, there is always a potential for misunderstanding between agencies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is important to communicate and this is, indeed, one of the lessons that we have learnt here – to be aware of whether what you are saying is understood in the same way by the person who is receiving it; and the person who is receiving it, should be aware that what he has received may not be what the person who communicated it intended.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is not just a function of the digital age or email or anything, I mean, we are all familiar with the old games that we play telephone or whatever it is, you pass the message and then by the time it reaches the 10th person, it is completely garbled.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is not a function of the digital age.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is a function of making sure that we communicate with each other clearly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, MDDI thought that the Bizfile portal, the search function was not a new use case whereas ACRA thought that, well, it is a new use case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Then, what do you do when you stop using partial?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Or have I to stop using partial now?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That depends on whether it was new or not new.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there are gaps in understanding and we just have to keep on working at them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, will Members who submit appeals to the Government on behalf of their constituents still be expected to submit their full NRIC numbers even when there is clearly no need for it, for instance, an appeal to the Land Transport Authority to construct lifts on a pedestrian overhead bridge?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if leaked NRIC numbers are found, will MDDI notify affected individuals and help them to mitigate risks, such as identity theft or fraud, for example, by offering affected individuals identity monitoring services, credit monitoring or fraud alerts to prevent misuse?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Perhaps, I will address the second point first and also, Dr Tan Wu Meng alluded to that because he talked about the collection and use of data, especially NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should point out, if the Member read Annex A, that you must expect your NRIC number to be known to quite a few people.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, I can still remember the NRIC number of some of my classmates and my National Service (NS) colleagues, because we used it all the time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And so, you must expect your NRIC number to be known to others.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: While it is private, you must expect that it is not secret.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is the status and how you should treat NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think the most important impact to assess on this case is what is the impact on the individual.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this case, when an individual incorporates a company, starts a business, he has to register with ACRA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And in his registration with ACRA, he knows that the details of himself and his company must be searchable and accessible for corporate transparency reasons.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, he knows that his NRIC number may be searchable and may be known to any number of people who want to find out about what his business associations are with various companies and what his associations with previous companies have been as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And so, the fact that his NRIC number has now become known is not in itself something which the individual should find unexpected or surprising.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The important thing for the individual is that he must not use his NRIC number in an inappropriate way, such as using it as an authenticator or as a password.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And if he does that, he is quite secure.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Giam asked whether or not we have looked at the dark web and so on, whether people are selling NRIC numbers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the question of collection and use of NRIC numbers, actually, in the communication with the Government agencies, I think it is important to know who you are communicating with.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: You are not communicating with an anonymous person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: You are communicating with a person who is your resident, who has a specific concern and therefore, should be prepared to identify himself and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think that is quite proper and quite legitimate, especially if the person is making a request or has an appeal to be made.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think that is quite proper and appropriate, and should continue.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have two clarifications for the Senior Minister, but I want to first thank the Panel for making such a thorough investigation in a relatively short time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to respect the two Ministers for taking the courage to assume responsibility and make public apologies very shortly after the incident broke.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I also want to empathise with the Public Service officers who have been involved.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I can imagine the guilt and stress that they must have gone through on discovering the mistakes and making right the processes for a live portal and the lessons learned.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also want to appreciate Senior Minister Teo for explaining rather complex issues and investigations in a very simple way for us to understand.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A follow-up question is that I have my IT-trained husband to thank for understanding the difference between an identifier and an authenticator in the use of NRIC number.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But in my conversations with many people from my constituency who have discussed about this whole incident, it actually takes some time for people to understand the difference because there is technicality involved.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And I am increasingly concerned about emerging issues in the related issues of personal data protection and privacy, cybersecurity and cybercrimes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The coordination, there needs to be — inter-Ministry and inter-agency coordination in the Government is emerging to be a difficult topic and a very technical one, and I take lessons from how we are dealing with climate change and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Ng, you may want to get to your clarifications.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Well, first, I want to thank Ms Ng Ling Ling for her comments on our officers and also on the Ministers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think they will appreciate your understanding and empathy with what they are going through right now.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have spoken to some of the officers myself and told them and assured them that if there is a shortcoming, we have to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I have assured them that we will deal with it fairly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On inter-Ministry coordination, there are a number of different levels.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We do have inter-Ministry committees and coordination mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Sometimes we are accused of having too many, but we do have quite a few of these.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These also have to operate at the appropriate level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the Senior Minister or Deputy Prime Minister level, they tend to deal more with policy and not implementation on a day-to-day or immediate basis, because if you try and do that kind of thing at the Senior Minister or Deputy Prime Minister level, you will end up not being successful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is the same answer as I gave with regard to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I mean he is responsible for everything, but if you refer everything to him, he will become the bottleneck and nothing will get done and things will get delayed.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, similarly, with coordination at the Deputy Prime Minister or Senior Minister level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And as Minister of State Sun Xueling has recounted, we actually have achieved a certain amount of success in getting the different agencies together at the implementation level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And so, you have to get things done at the correct level; so now, we are able to actually swing into action much faster.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, I think it was The Economist which commended us on being able to do this where other countries have not.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But if you try to do that kind of coordination and day-to-day action at the Deputy Prime Minister or Senior Minister level, I think you will end up with a very, very major bottleneck and it will not work properly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, you have to do it at the correct level and we do that for cybercrime, we do that for cybersecurity as well, and we have similar structures.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And therefore, since they were using the NRIC number as an authenticator they came to believe that the NRIC number should be kept secret.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, if you ask me for my NRIC number, I would not tell you.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But actually, you have to tell the person, because that is the way in which you can be definitively referred to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Otherwise, how do you refer to yourself definitively?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there was a contradiction in the individuals' minds as to what the NRIC number is.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And when some organisations and people started to use the NRIC number as an authenticator, they began to say, "Well, then I should keep it secret".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But that is not the original purpose of the NRIC number.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I said, we used to use it all the time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I still remember the NRIC numbers of my classmates and my NS colleagues.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is the proper use of the NRIC and it should be sensitive, but you must assume that it is not secret.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, you were not here when Senior Minister Teo started his address and you would also not have heard my comments earlier.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Yes, but when the Senior Minister was addressing the House, you were not in the Chamber, when we started.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I have read the report very thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The report shows that this NRIC number incident is a communication disaster of the Government, both internally and externally.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For such a major change in policy which pertains to —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you have six clarifications, by all means, ask all six.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But if preambles are needed, you heard me earlier and you said you heard me, there is no need to make too much preamble.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If the clarifications can be just asked, that will be appreciated and that is required.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister whether any of these senior leaders have voiced concerns over the CM?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And when did the political office holders first get involved in the inter-agency response to the feedback and media queries on Bizfile?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Was there any direction provided by the political office holders over the inter-agency response and the decision to disable the People Search function in Bizfile?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: To many Singaporeans, including myself, the new policy does not make sense in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: To many Singaporeans, including myself, the new policy does not make sense in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I agree with the Government that NRIC numbers, full or masked, should not be used as authentication, and that must be impressed on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next question, why is there a need to do away with the masked NRIC policy?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Given that it is still an added security measure, as an identifier, and is already an established practice?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Next question, has the Government considered that this policy reversal could be very confusing for Singaporeans, especially those that are not digitally-literate?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Many Singaporeans have raised concerns over whether our full NRIC numbers have been so compromised that there is no need to mask them anymore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, my last question is, can Senior Minister confirm, whether there is any evidence to show that our full NRIC numbers have been compromised on a large scale already?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is the same question that Mr Giam had asked me and I think I have given the reply.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this idea that full NRIC numbers are compromised, I think it starts from the wrong basis, which I have tried very hard to explain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Your NRIC number is supposed to be known by those people who need to know it and so you must expect that your NRIC number is known to quite a few others.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is why it should not be used as an authenticator.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And it is, in fact, not easy to communicate this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is why we have to do this in a very careful process and in part, it is partially the reason why we have this misunderstanding and gap in communication, even within the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I think it is something which should be done, particularly to protect those who are not digitally-savvy, who go away with the idea that, "Yes, my NRIC number is secret.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Therefore, I can use it as a password.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And partial NRIC number is very good, because it hides my real NRIC number, which should be secret." So, we should move away from that, especially to protect those who are not digitally-savvy, because they may not fully appreciate the unsafe nature and the dangers of doing that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Then, he asked when the political office holders got involved in the public communications on the Bizfile portal issue.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They got involved, I think, almost as soon as it became apparent that there was public anxiety.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Next question about paragraph 40 and the email to senior officers, yes, the July 2024 CM was emailed to officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Well, in the process of putting in new directives or new circular memos, and so on, there is a process in which the agencies who put this out and who are responsible for that domain area, communicate with the agencies which may be impacted, implementing agencies and so on; and MDDI did do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think I have answered all of Mr Leong's questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could I just quickly confirm that it is the official position of the Government that it will, going forward, be actively working to discourage or dissuade the private sector's use of NRIC numbers in all authentication use cases, including the protection of confidential, but not necessarily secret information, such as, for example, health reports or bank statements?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I say this fully appreciating the distinction between identification and authentication, but nevertheless, caution against going overboard in pursuing best practice security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because after all, it is not complicated for IT personnel to happily code up password hashes, but the consequences for the rest of us could be a much diminished user experience – needing to cross reference one-time passwords each time we wish to do something simple like retrieving our bank statement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Could I make a clarification that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is suggesting that the Public Service should not adopt best practice security processes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, I am asking, with regard to how the Government will now recommend private sector action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, in terms of how it will dissuade the private sector from using these kinds of authentication method.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Assoc Prof Lim did not answer my question.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I thought I heard him say that we should not be adopting best practices.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I want to confirm whether he thinks we should be adopting best practices or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I got one final clarification for the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I still want to ask whether it is a better communication strategy and also maybe a better strategy in getting Singaporeans to not use their NRIC number, whether full or masked, for authentication, by just educating them on not using it for authentication.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Rather than introducing one more factor, and say that, "Oh, we should discontinue the masked NRIC also".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because there are some advantages to the use of the masked NRIC.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think, Mr Leong, yes, you have asked your clarification.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I hope that in his ability to communicate with the public that he will also stress that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is an important message which all of us should take to the public, including Mr Leong.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I also hope that he has read the Annex A and listened to my explanations as to why the use of partial NRIC numbers, in the belief that they provide adequate definitive identification, or that they are safe because it protects your NRIC number, which people mistakenly believe that it should be secret and cannot be revealed to anybody, that this is also the wrong belief.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I understand that the second part is indeed more difficult to explain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, in the implementation, when we do this communication, I think I do agree with him – the more urgent and important thing is to tell people, "Do not use your NRIC number for authentication or as your password".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think that is the most important thing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And then, we will have to shift people away from the idea that if you use the partial NRIC number, it is enough to identify you.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And the idea that if you use your partial NRIC number, it somehow keeps your NRIC number "secret", which is not so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that part, I think it will have to be a follow-up on the first part.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But as I said, and I thank Members for their support, that we will deal with them fairly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This has been and will continue to be the Government's approach when mistakes are made or shortcomings are identified from time to time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is an approach which this Government is determined to continue, and it is a key pillar of good governance and for the good of Singapore and our people.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will now go back into the Committee of Supply to debate the Estimates.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have revised the commencement time of the Committee of Supply to start immediately.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Hon Members will be notified of the revised conclusion times for the subsequent Heads of Expenditure.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now read the Order of the day.
